processing: A green tea of tender spring leaf, finished into tight, curled, downy strands. The details of firing vary by maker, but the kill-green keeps the leaf unoxidised as in other Sichuan greens.
harvest_season: Between the spring equinox and Guyu (late March to about 20 April), mainly one bud with one leaf and a little one bud with two just opening.
appearance_dry: Tight, curled strands with visible down, tender green and glossy.
appearance_wet: Pale green, tender and even leaves.
taste_profile: Rich aroma and a full, brisk, clean cup, as Sichuan descriptions of the tea put it; expect the fresh vegetal sweetness usual for a spring green.

brewing.notes: A general method for tender spring green tea: glass or porcelain, water well off the boil, leaf left uncovered so it does not stew.

vintage_note: Like other Chinese spring greens it is normally bought as the current year's harvest and drunk within about a year. Earlier spring lots usually carry the higher price. It is not a tea to age.
description:
Wenjun green tea comes from Qionglai in Sichuan, and takes its name from Zhuo Wenjun, the Western Han woman from this town who is remembered for eloping with the poet Sima Xiangru. The name is a local tribute; the tea itself is a plain, well-made spring green.

It is picked young, mostly a bud and one leaf, and shaped into tight curled strands with the down still showing. That young material gives the glossy tender colour of the dry leaf and the bright green liquor.

In the cup it is described as strongly fragrant and brisk rather than delicate. As with most tender greens, the usual mistake is water that is too hot or a steep that runs long, so start cooler and pour off in good time.

Buy the latest spring and ask for the picking date. Qionglai also has a well-known dark tea tradition, so check the category on the packet when you see the Wenjun name.
history:
Qionglai's Wenjun green tea was rated a national famous tea in 1985 and 1989, and collected provincial famous-tea titles during the 1990s. The story of Zhuo Wenjun explains the name only: she lived in the Western Han, and the tea as sold today is a modern named product.

The town still points visitors to the Wenjun Well and the Qintai, the sites tied to her story, and the tea borrows that fame.
